segments.text: Andrej Karpathy once made his model train 25% faster by adding 47 words to its vocabulary,
which is the list of words the model knows. These were words the model will never use.
He changed one number, 50,257 to 50,304, and hit run.
Adding junk to a model should not make it faster, which is why this looks like a typo.
It isn't one, and the reason shows what a GPU actually spends its day doing.
A GPU is a dumb chip with one trick, which is running the same small job
on thousands of pieces of data at once. Picture a kitchen. The CPU is one very good chef,
and the GPU is a thousand line cooks who all read the same card which says to chop an onion.
Each cook has a different onion, and none of them needs to be clever because there are so many of
them. The card is called a kernel. It has nothing to do with a Jupiter kernel or the operating
system kernel, and yes, the naming is unfortunate. Say we want to add two lists of 262,144 numbers each.
The GPU starts that many cooks, and each one finds its own position,
so cook number 5000 takes the 5000th item from each list and adds the pair. No cook knows the
others exist. The cooks work at stations, which on the chip are called streaming multi-processors.
An A100, a common data center GPU, has 108 of them, and an H100, its newest sibling, has 132.
Cooks arrive at a station in groups, and a group stays there until it finishes. The chip runs fast
only when every station is busy, and there are three ways for a station to sit idle.
The first way is that the work doesn't divide evenly across the stations.
Most of what a neural network does is multiply matrices, and a matrix is just a big grid of
numbers. Multiplying two of them produces a third grid, and every cell in that grid needs its own pile
of multiplying and adding, which is exactly the kind of job a thousand cooks can split up.
To split it, the GPU cuts the answer grid into tiles, which are rectangles of cells,
and gives each tile to one group of cooks. Groups go out in rounds. With 108 stations
and 108 tiles, everything finishes in one round. Add one more tile, 109 in total,
and the first 108 go out together while the last one runs alone in a second round,
with 107 stations standing around. That is under 1% more work for nearly double the time.
Something has to decide how the tiles get cut, and that job belongs to a library,
which is a shelf of ready-made code. This one is called Cublas, and we can think of it as a cookbook
with many versions of the same card, each tuned for a different size of order. It looks at the
matrix sizes and hands out the card that suits them. On an A100, the fast cards are built
around chunks of 64, so a size that leaves a ragged edge pushes the library onto a slower card.
This is what happened in Carpathi's case. A language model ends by scoring every word in
its vocabulary to pick the next one, and that scoring is one of these matrix multiplications,
with the vocabulary size on one side of the grid.
50,257 does not divide evenly by 64, which got him a slow card, and 50,304 is 64 times 786,
which got him a fast one. The 47 extra words cost almost nothing,
and the kernel change was worth 25%. The practical version is to pad sizes up
to a multiple of 64. That applies to the vocabulary and to the hidden size,
which is the width of the model's inner layers. Padding costs a little memory and often helps,
though the best multiple depends on the GPU and on how many bits each number uses.
The second way is that the cooks are waiting for ingredients.
The data sits in main memory, which is a pantry down the hall. Every kernel walks there for its
inputs and walks back with the result, and one trip takes hundreds of times longer than one chop.
The chip does have a little counter space right next to the stations,
and anything left there can be grabbed instantly. What matters is how much chopping happens per
trip. A big matrix multiply is a cook who carries back a whole crate and chops all day. Small steps
are a cook who walks to the pantry, chops once, and walks back. Those small steps include relu,
which zeroes out negative numbers, normalisation, which we scales numbers to a standard range,
and softmax, which turns scores into percentages. In BERT, a well-known language model,
those steps made up about 0.2% of the math and over a third of the time.
Take any two small steps in a row, say cosine and then cosine again. As two kernels,
that makes four trips, which are fetch, put back, fetch again, and put back.
Merged into one kernel, the middle result stays on the counter, and it makes two trips,
which runs about twice as fast. This is called fusion. Plain PyTorch, the most common toolkit
for building models in Python, runs one operation at a time and cannot see what comes next,
so it cannot fuse them. Torch.compile is a compiler, which is a program that reads
our instructions and rearranges them before anything runs. It reads the whole model first,
like a chef who reads the full recipe before starting, and merges what it can,
and we turn it on with one line. The third way is that nobody hands the cooks a job.
The CPU is the chef calling out orders, and it does that through Python,
the language most of this code is written in, which is slow. In the time Python adds two
numbers, an A100 could do almost 10 million calculations. Big orders hide the delay,
because the cooks are still busy when the next one arrives. Tiny orders do not,
because the cooks finish and then wait for the next shout. Horace, he has an easy test for
whether this is happening, which is to double the batch size, meaning the number of examples
the model handles at once, or, in kitchen terms, the number of onions in each order.
If a step gets only 10% slower, we doubled the work and barely paid for it,
which means the chef was the bottleneck. The remedy is a CUDA graph. CUDA is NVIDIA's toolkit
for giving orders to the GPU, and a graph is a routine written down once, so the kitchen
can run its start to finish in a single launch. Torch.compile with the mode set to reduce overhead
sets one up for us. When training feels slow, the first thing most of us do is run
NVIDIA SMI. It prints a status panel for the GPU, showing memory in use, temperature,
power draw and a number called utilisation, which is meant to say how busy the GPU is.
That utilisation number is the one that fools us. We have all seen it say 100% while training
crawls. It only means a kernel was running at that moment, and one kernel, using a handful
of cooks running non-stop, reads 100% while the kitchen is nearly empty. It works like the
open light on a kitchen door, which says nothing about how many cooks are working.
To see what is really happening, we record a trace with the PyTorch profiler. A trace works
like a security camera over the kitchen, showing each kernel with its duration plus the gaps where
nothing ran at all. Writing our own kernels is probably not worth it, though some teams
do it anyway. Unsloft, a tool for fine-tuning models, which means adjusting an existing model
on new examples, wrote its own kernels and trained about twice as fast as the usual hugging-face
setup. Marlin is a kernel for models whose numbers are squeezed down to 4 bits to save memory,
and inside VLLM, a popular program for serving models, it ran about 10 times faster than a
basic 4-bit kernel in one test. Those teams sell speed, so the effort pays for them.
For the rest of us, the libraries already ship good kernels. The first step is to read a profile,
which tells us whether the problem is ragged sizes, pantry trips or a slow chef,
and torch.compile comes after that. A compiler merges what we wrote
and cannot invent a better way to do the math. Flash attention shows the difference.
Attention is the step where a model compares every word with every other word,
which produces a huge table of scores, and researchers rewrote it so the table is built
in small pieces on the counter and never makes the trip to the pantry. That took a human idea.
Kernels are also code, and code has bugs. In 2025, Anthropic found a compiler bug on TPUs,
which are Google's own kind of AI chip, that made one kernel sometimes drop the
most likely next word from the shortlist Claude picks from and answer quality suffered until it
was fixed. We are already choosing kernels every time we type a batch size,
a sequence length or a vocabulary size. That means how many examples we process at once,
how long each example is and how many words the model knows. And each number decides which
kernel runs and how many stations it fills. Carpathi got a 25% speed up from 47 words
nobody will read.
